title: WTA Finals: Mirra Andreeva eliminates Jessica Pegula to reach final, winning in straight sets after 'diva' criticism
article_text:
Mirra Andreeva took a straight-sets victory over Jessica Pegula at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells.

Andreeva's 6-3 6-4 victory saw her advance to the final at the year-end tournament in California, making her the first teenager to reach the title match at the WTA Finals since 2004.

Andreeva and Pegula were playing one another for the first time in their careers and their match-up in the last four came after Pegula had been picked up on a hot mic criticising Andreeva at the start of the tournament.

In a livestreamed practice session, Pegula was heard labelling Andreeva a "diva" who "needs to be humbled".

Andreeva had the last word as she eliminated the American from the tournament. To win Andreeva had to come back from being a break down in both sets.

Pegula broke first in the opening set but Andreeva immediately responded to force a break back her way.

Andreeva smashed a forehand cross-court to claim another break and leave her serving for the set.

She managed to see it out, but only after Pegula squandered a break point.

In the second set another break of serve saw Andreeva move 5-3 up and enjoy control of the contest. Pegula did hold serve after that but Andreeva closed out the contest in her next service game.

"It was a tough match," Andreeva said. "You have to work hard to win a point against her. She is going to leave everything out there and make your life complicated, so I wanted to make her life complicated as well today."

Andreeva, appearing in the WTA Finals for the first time, has not dropped a set in four matches at the event so far.

Ukraine's Elina Svitolina will meet Andreeva in the final after she dismantled the reigning Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

Svitolina won 6-2 6-1, winning rapidly and almost shutting Noskova entirely out of the second set.

The Andreeva-Svitolina final will be a rematch after the two played each other earlier in this competition format. Since losing to the Russian in the group stage of these WTA Finals, Svitolina has staged an extraordinary resurgence and was in outstanding form by the time she met Noskova in their semi-final.

title: Yee Hern-Vannee capture maiden World Tour title at Kaohsiung Masters
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Wee Yee Hern-Vannee Gobi captured their first World Tour title together after winning the Super 100 Kaohsiung Masters mixed doubles final in Taiwan on Sunday.

The world No. 83 defeated South Korea's world No. 289 Ki Dong Ju-Jeong Na Eun 24-22, 21-17 at the Kaohsiung Arena.

It was a breakthrough for Yee Hern-Vannee, who were playing in their first World Tour final together, against a pair featuring Paris 2024 Olympic silver medallist Na Eun.

The fourth seeds had reached the final after beating Taiwan's Lin Sheng Ming-Sun Liang Ching 21-11, 11-21, 21-8 in the semi-finals.

title: How prize money and ranking points will be awarded at the 2026 ATP Finals
article_text:
After a long and demanding season, eight of the best male tennis players in the world head to Turin for the ATP Finals.

Two-time defending champion Jannik Sinner will not be action in 2026 but there is still a strong field in Turin, led by world No 1 Alexander Zverev and world No 3 Carlos Alcaraz.

They are joined by Daniil Medvedev and Ben Shelton, while Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Frances Tiafoe, and Rafael Jodar all make their debut appearances at the year-end championships.

There is plenty at stake at the final ATP event of 2026 and, with action getting underway, here is all you need to know about the prize money and ranking points on offer.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

Hugely significant ranking points are on offer at the ATP Finals in 2026, with a total of 1,500 points on offer for an unbeaten champion in Turin — the most ranking points available at any tournament outside of the four Grand Slams.

No ranking points are on offer merely for qualifying for the event, meaning all eight men in singles action will have to win at least one match to earn ranking points.

Each round-robin match is worth 200 ranking points, meaning a player who wins all three round-robin matches will have 600 ranking points to their name at that stage of the tournament.

A player with two wins and one defeat will have 400 ranking points, while a player with one win and two defeats will have 200 ranking points to their name.

In the knockout phase, the two victorious semi-finalists will both earn a further 400 ranking points, though the two beaten players will not add any further points to their round-robin total.

Whoever wins the final will then take home a further 500 ranking points on top of the 400 points from the semi-final, and whatever they won during the round-robin stage.

As confirmed earlier this week, there is a total prize money pot of $15,750,000 in Turin this year, on offer across both the singles and doubles tournaments.

While the eight singles players don’t automatically earn ranking points for qualification, they will all receive a base participation fee of $338,000 if they complete all three round-robin matches.

After that, each round-robin win is then worth a further $405,000 per match in the singles competition.

If a player was to win all three matches in the round-robin stage, they would have already earned an impressive $1,553,000 in prize money ahead of the semi-final stage, including the participation fee.

The two beaten semi-finalists will not earn any further prize money on top of their round-robin total, though the two victorious players will both earn a further $1,206,000.

The victorious finalist and eventual champion will then earn a staggering $2,412,000 for their victory in the final, on top of the $1,206,000 won in the semi-final and their earnings from the round-robin stage.

An unbeaten champion would take home a staggering $5,171,000, potentially one of the biggest prize money payouts ever awarded in the sport.

title: Kumamoto Masters: New Combo Tastes Success Yet Again
article_text:
Malaysia’s Aaron Tai and Yap Roy King won their second title from just five tournaments together, as they outplayed home hopes Takuro Hoki/Yugo Kobayashi in the final of the Kumamoto Masters Japan 2026.

The world No.57, who won their first tournament as a pair last month, have been on a strong run, having made the semifinals at the HYLO Open a fortnight ago. Today they were able to negate the greater experience of Hoki and Kobayashi with a sharp attacking game, peppered with some spectacular shots.

While Tai was his usual bustling self at the net, Yap’s big hitting from the back powered the Malaysians to a comfortable win in the decider: 16-21 21-13 21-15.

That was the second setback for the hosts on the day, after Koki Watanabe had fallen to Lakshya Sen in the men’s singles final.

Both are in a close race for the HSBC BWF World Tour Finals; with his win, Sen moved ahead of Watanabe, but it will still come down to the Hong Kong Open next week.

Sen had a slow start, but once he found his rhythm, he moved fluidly and exploded into precise smashes that often found the lines. As the match wore on Watanabe couldn’t keep pace, and he eventually fell 13-21 21-18 21-14. It was Sen’s second successive title after winning the HYLO Open.

“It feels very good to win a title here,” said the Indian. “Last year I played the semifinals, so I’m happy that I bettered it this time. Second title back-to-back, I would love to continue this form.

“The sides were difficult because of the wind. I just kept my confidence in the second game. I was trying to keep a good length and keep attacking.

“I will be fighting for the World Tour Finals. This tournament will help me get good points for that. I have one more to go, the Hong Kong Open. I’m just keeping my confidence up, even though I’ve had tough matches, so it’s really good that I kept believing in myself.”

» Top seed Akane Yamaguchi continued her recent dominance over Wang Zhi Yi, beating the second seed 21-14 22-20 for her fourth title of the season.

» Rin Iwanaga/Kie Nakanishi picked up their first title of the year – and their first since the Denmark Open two years ago – beating compatriots Ririna Hiramoto/Chiharu Shida 21-19 21-15. Iwanaga/Nakanishi have qualified to the World Tour Finals.

» In the mixed doubles final, Jiang Zhen Bang/Wei Ya Xin beat compatriots Gao Jia Xuan/Wu Meng Ying 15-21 21-15 21-14 for their fifth title from the last six tournaments.

title: Rio Marathon Names TCS as Official AI and Technology Partner
article_text:
Rio Marathon has partnered with TCS as its official AI and Technology Partner, enhancing race operations, runner experiences, and digital innovation.

In the recent sports business news, Rio Marathon has signed a partnership with Tata Consultancy Services, naming it the official AI and Technology Partner of the event. This partnership represents a major achievement in the international sports sponsorship plan of TCS and showcases its dedication to sports, health, and technology through the largest street running race in Latin America.

TCS will leverage its capabilities in AI, data analytics and digital transformation technologies to help enhance the technical side of the marathon, particularly with respect to improving efficiency and the runner and spectator experience. This collaboration is taking place as the Rio Marathon is establishing itself as an international event. The 2026 marathon featured participation from around 70,000 people in four different race formats and created a new high in economic impact for the city, worth R$711 million.

Our running journey has a new destination: Rio de Janeiro.🏃 We’re marking our first marathon partnership in Latin America as the Official AI and Technology Partner of the @maratonadorio. The partnership extends our global running portfolio to 14 leading events, engaging nearly 700,000 runners each year. And what better time to join the journey, with the race set to celebrate its 25th anniversary in 2027. We’ll bring our expertise in AI, data analytics and digital innovation to help create a more connected and engaging experience for runners and spectators. More details here: https://t.co/fFEArSBDSe With you for the long run, now in Rio.🏃♀️

Furthermore, the Rio Marathon also earned its first-ever World Athletics Elite Label in 2026, and were listed as one of the top ten marathon brands in the world by Brand Finance’s Marathons 50 rankings. TCS will leverage its experience in some of the biggest marathons around the world.

Commenting on this agreement, Duda Magalhães, president of Dream Factory, said, "It is an honour to welcome TCS as a partner of the Rio Marathon. Having a company by our side that is already connected to the world’s major marathons reinforces the scale the event has achieved, as well as our ambition to progress even further."

He further said, "Today, the Rio Marathon ranks among the ten strongest marathon brands globally and is currently experiencing a significant phase of expansion and international recognition. This partnership combines the strength of our platform with TCS’s global expertise in technology and innovation, creating new opportunities to enhance the runners’ experience and expand our presence on the world stage.”

Abhinav Kumar, Chief Marketing and Communications Officer at TCS, said, “Our global marathon sponsorships have become a cornerstone of the TCS brand and how we activate it with our clients, colleagues and communities. We are proud of the fact that our partner races create US$ 3.2 billion of economic uplift, improve wellbeing and raise crucial funds for charities."

He further said, "Expanding this strategy to the Rio Marathon makes for a natural evolution, given our growing presence in the Latin America region and the race’s own evolution into one of the top 10 brands in this sport. The iconic city of Rio de Janeiro and its marathon have grand ambitions ahead, and we are with them for the long run.”

In addition, the collaboration demonstrates the increased brand influence of TCS's sports portfolio. Having sponsored 14 of the world's most prestigious running competitions, which include five of the eight Abbott World Marathon Majors, the corporation has been able to interact with about 700,000 runners annually all over the world.

According to Brand Finance's Marathons 50 2026 report, the brand influence through sponsorships is extremely measurable and industry-leading. In 2025, TCS-sponsored races have managed to create an amazing $3.2 billion worth of economic impact for their host communities and represent 53% of the total created by the world's top 50 marathons.

title: Sportico: NBA teams took in $13.7B of a $14.5B 2025-26
article_text:
Sportico: NBA 2025-26 revenue $14.5B; teams got $13.7B

Sportico estimates the NBA made about $14.5 billion in 2025-26, with the 30 clubs taking in $13.7 billion, or $456 million apiece. Team revenue ranged from $895 million for Golden State to $339 million for Memphis, both after revenue sharing. Media-rights payouts rise about 7% a year on average. Local business—tickets, sponsorships and arena events—helps explain much of the gap between clubs.

This story was produced through MarketScale. See how Sports & Entertainment teams put it to work with Events & Onsite Capture.

Sportico's Kurt Badenhausen published a full breakdown of NBA finances on October 20. He puts the NBA's 2025-26 revenue at roughly $14.5 billion. The 30 clubs took in $13.7 billion of that, or $456 million apiece.

The team total includes concerts and other non-NBA events at arenas the clubs own or run. The league keeps part of the $14.5 billion at its own level to cover investments and expenses. For anyone who sells to, sponsors or operates alongside an NBA club, the more useful question is where the new money came from. Most of it came from a single contract.

The last figure is the one finance teams will care about most. Payouts rise about 7% a year on average, so the largest single line in a club's budget can be modeled a decade out. Gate receipts can't. Ticket money depends on who wins. The TV escalator doesn't.

The baseline helps here. In 2022, Front Office Sports reported that media rights made up roughly $2.6 billion of the league's annual revenue. The new deals are worth $6.9 billion a year, more than two and a half times that figure.

Sportico says the new media deal pushes the NBA closer to the NFL's economic model.

Sportico's latest estimates put NBA teams' combined revenue at $13.7 billion, above MLB clubs at $13.2 billion. The baseball figures cover the 2025 calendar season and the basketball figures cover 2025-26, which is the closest like-for-like comparison available.

For sponsorship and partnership teams, the share tells you more than the total. With 41% coming from central revenue, the remaining 59% (our arithmetic) is the local business the club sells itself: tickets, suites, sponsorships, concessions, merchandise, local media and arena events. A brand buying a team partnership deals with that local side. And that side explains the gap between the league's top and bottom clubs.

Team revenue ranged from $895 million for the Golden State Warriors to $339 million for the Memphis Grizzlies. Both figures are after revenue sharing, which moved roughly $400 million to lower-revenue teams. High-revenue clubs and 50% of luxury tax proceeds fund that pool.

Sportico's $13.7 billion team figure is net of revenue sharing and includes non-NBA events, such as concerts, at buildings teams own or operate. The $14.5 billion league figure is larger because part of it stays with the league for investments and expenses.

Golden State is a different case. The Warriors' revenue rose from $833 million in 2024-25 to $895 million in 2025-26, the most in the league in both seasons. Brady Klopfer of Golden State of Mind points to Chase Center, the privately funded arena the ownership group built in 2019. By building it, he writes, the Warriors have become the landlords to the biggest concerts in the Bay Area, with Doja Cat, Phoebe Bridgers, the Jonas Brothers and Journey booked in the coming weeks. It is also home to the WNBA's Golden State Valkyries, a separate entity under the same ownership that Sportico values at $850 million.

Golden State led the league with $895 million in team revenue in 2025-26, according to Sportico. When a club controls its building and keeps it busy on non-game nights, local revenue can grow faster than the league's shared money.

Memphis shows the other side. The Grizzlies had the lowest revenue in Sportico's figures in both seasons, at $301 million in 2024-25 and $339 million in 2025-26. Those totals are net of revenue sharing. High-revenue teams and 50% of luxury tax proceeds paid for that system, which sent roughly $400 million to low-revenue teams. The same per-team national TV payout is a much larger share of a $339 million budget than of an $895 million one.

Local media was a weak point in 2024-25. Sportico reported that basketball-related income came to $10.25 billion that season. That figure, which determines the salary cap, was held down by a choppy local media market and by several small-market teams advancing to the conference finals, which reduced postseason gate receipts. Because of that, teams received more than $480 million from the escrow fund, which exists to keep revenue divided 51-49 between players and owners. Partners with deals tied to regional broadcast inventory should keep a close eye on the local media numbers.

The league has global ambitions, including plans to build new leagues in Africa and Europe, and it has a new blockbuster TV contract. Together, those have led investors to push up the price of owning 1/30th of it. Sportico puts the average franchise at $6.64 billion, up 21% in a year and 157% from $2.58 billion in 2021. Memphis, the lowest-valued club, is worth $4.2 billion, 2.8 times its 2021 value of $1.51 billion.

According to signals from the league, a call on expansion franchises in Las Vegas and Seattle should come before the year ends. One detail is worth tracking: Sportico's $281 million per-team TV projection assumes a 30-team league. If the league grows to 32 teams, that assumption no longer holds.

title: Owen Farrell takes on first coaching role as England legend reveals retirement ambition
article_text:
Former England captain Owen Farrell has taken another step towards a career in coaching, combining his playing duties with a role at Saracens.

The 35-year-old has been helping coach the Premiership club during the PREM Rugby Cup, including their remarkable 96-42 victory over Northampton Saints.

And while Farrell isn't ready to hang up his boots, he's already thinking about what comes next.

Now he's getting a proper taste of life on the other side of the touchline.

Speaking to TNT Sports, Farrell confirmed he had been involved in coaching last season and was enjoying the opportunity to do more.

"We've had one week of PREM Cup, so I did a little bit of that last year and am doing the same this year, so I'm loving that. I'm really interested in it."

Farrell has been juggling both responsibilities, switching between coaching and playing depending on Saracens' schedule.

When cup fixtures arrive, he steps into the coaching setup while continuing his own training.

But when Premiership rugby returns, his attention switches back to playing.

"I've been all in, in either [playing and coaching]," he explained.

The experienced fly-half is clearly enjoying seeing the game from a different perspective.

However, he remains determined to make the most of his remaining playing career.

Could Farrell follow his father into coaching?

Few players have spent more time directing teammates than Farrell.

The 112-cap England international has built his reputation on leadership, tactical awareness and demanding the highest standards.

Now he's getting the opportunity to pass that knowledge on.

His father, Andy Farrell, has already established himself as one of international rugby's leading coaches.

The Ireland boss made the transition from playing to coaching and went on to lead the British & Irish Lions.

Owen could eventually follow a similar path.

Saracens have already recognised his coaching potential, with the club confirming his involvement during the opening rounds of the PREM Rugby Cup.

Whether that eventually leads to a role with England remains to be seen.

But Farrell's next chapter is already taking shape.

The boots aren't being packed away just yet, but the coaching tracksuit is getting plenty of use.

title: Canada overcome ‘tough’ start to claim their biggest win of 2026
article_text:
Canada have bounced back from a heavy defeat to Georgia in the World Rugby Nations Cup with a statement 38-17 victory against Hong Kong China, who have also secured their place at Men’s Rugby World Cup 2027 in Australia.

It’s the biggest win of the international season for the Canadians, who have now improved their record to 2-2-1 in the Nations Cup. But the USA Eagles can’t be caught in Pool B, securing top spot with one round still to play.

The Canadians were coming off a 45-point defeat to eventual Pool A champions Georgia, which was their equal biggest defeat of 2026. But Canada bounced back in a big way against Hong Kong China, piling on 33 unanswered points during the final 30 minutes.

Canada went down to 14 men during the first half after outside centre Isaac Olsen was shown a yellow card, but the North American side remained in the contest. Hong Kong China led 10-0 deep in the first half, before winger Nic Benn hit back for Canada.

Five points separated the teams at half-time, and Hong Kong China were actually the first to strike during the second term as well. But it was one-way point-scoring traffic from then on, with utility back Takoda McMullin starring during the second 40.

“We work really hard and we play to earn victories on the weekend. It felt like last weekend’s performance, especially the second half, wasn’t reflective of us as a team,” first-time Canada captain Ben LeSage said post-game.

“To come out today, to have a really tough first 20 minutes, Hong Kong [China] really battled against us, kudos to them.

“The second half, you finally saw the type of rugby we’re trying to play and a bit of confidence. Really proud of the guys.”

It was a one-score game at half-time, but a focus on getting “back to basics” helped Canada take control of the contest. Canada finished with 71 per cent possession in the final 10 minutes, and scored 12 points during that same period.

Backrower Josh Hrstich conceded a yellow card and Hong Kong China went down to 14 men around the 50-minute mark, with a penalty try also going in favour of the Canadians. It was a three-point game and the Canadians appeared supremely confident from there.

Spencer Jones, Sam Miller and McMullin all made their mark with a five-pointer each as Canada ran out big winners in the end. Canada now prepare to face Romania next weekend, in the final round of the Nations Cup.

“We had to play quick ball. We had to take care of the ball in the ruck. We wanted to get fast ball and we wanted to the space you saw, starting to put the ball in behind a bit and play in the right areas of the field,” LeSage added.

“It’s something that we talk about all week but it’s hard to do on game day under pressure. You saw it start to come to fruition in the second half.”

title: Harry Hockings red card: Why was the Japan lock sent off against England?
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The second row made direct contact with his shoulder to the head of English ball carrier Ellis Genge as he attempted to make a hit on the loosehead prop.

Referee Damian Schneider, in consultation with television match official (TMO) Marius van der Westhuizen, quickly deemed that the incident met the yellow card threshold, with foul play review officer Aled Griffiths upgrading the sanction to a 20-minute red card.

The challenge was deemed to be a high degree of danger with no mitigation. Under World Rugby rules, Japan are permitted to replace Hockings after that 20-minute period has elapsed.

But what are the laws around head contact that referees are following and how do they decide on the punishment? Here’s everything you need to know:

What are World Rugby’s laws on head contact?

Head-on-head contact in the tackle comes under Law 9 of the Laws of Rugby Union, which covers foul play.

Law 9.11 dictates “Players must not do anything that is reckless or dangerous to others, including leading with the elbow or forearm, or jumping into, or over, a tackler” and Law 9.13 goes on to say “A player must not tackle an opponent early, late or dangerously. Dangerous tackling includes, but is not limited to, tackling or attempting to tackle an opponent above the line of the shoulders even if the tackle starts below the line of the shoulders.”

If a player breaks these laws and the act is deemed to be reckless or dangerous, then the referee is entitled to issue a yellow or red card.

World Rugby also clarify the intent of the laws, stating in their guidelines that: “Player welfare drives World Rugby’s decision making for zero tolerance of foul play, especially where head contact occurs. The focus must be on the actions of those involved, not the injury – the need for an HIA [a Head Injury Assessment] does not necessarily mean that there has been illegal head contact.”

What are the punishments for head-on-head contact?

Ok, this is where things get technical and debates start to occur. In March 2023, World Rugby issued their latest ‘head contact process law application guidelines’ to guide referees on whether foul play has occurred and how it should be punished.

The referee has to go through a four-step process (detailed below) to determine the extent of the foul play and the sanction. The four steps are:

Step 1 (has head contact occurred?) is relatively straightforward, with head contact including the head and the face as well as the neck and throat area. If any head contact is made at all, we move on to Step 2.

Step 2 (was there foul play?) is a touch more complex. The referees are told to consider whether the head contact was either intentional, reckless or avoidable – e.g. the defender is always upright. If it was, the tackler will be penalised and they move on to Step 3. However, if the head contact was deemed not to be foul play, the game continues.

Step 3 (what was the degree of danger?) – judged from high to low – determines the initial punishment.

A degree of high danger is judged on any of: direct contact rather than indirect, a high-force impact, a lack of control from the tackler, the incident occurring at high speed, the tackler leading with the head/shoulder/elbow/forearm or the tackle being reckless. If the referee judges there to be a high degree of danger, a red card will be shown.

Meanwhile, low danger is judged as indirect contact, low force, low speed or no leading head/shoulder/forearm/swinging arm and a yellow card or even just a penalty to the opposition may be awarded.

The final step, Step 4 (is there any mitigation?) determines whether the punishment can be reduced by one grade (i.e red card down to yellow card or yellow card down to just a penalty). Mitigation includes a sudden or significant drop in height or change in direction from ball carrier, a late change in dynamics due to another player in the contact area, a clear effort from the tackler to reduce their height or the tackler having no time to adjust.

However, mitigation will never apply for intentional or always-illegal acts of foul play.

What about the Foul Play Review Officer/Bunker review?

Introduced ahead of the 2023 Men’s Rugby World Cup was the Bunker review system. This allows the referee to issue a yellow card to a player, sending them to the sin-bin while play goes on, where a Foul Play Review Official (FPRO) will then take another look at the incident and determine if the yellow card should be upgraded to red, allowing the game to continue rather than a long stoppage to debate this.

The referee crosses their arms to indicate a Bunker review will take place.

Once a player is in the sin-bin, the FPRO has up to eight minutes to review the decision and decide if it warrants upgrading to a red card. If not, the player will return to the field after their 10 minutes in the sin-bin has elapsed.

Referees have the option to award a 20-minute red card for technical offences. Any act of foul play which is deemed not deliberate or intentional will now see the player punished with a 20-minute red card rather than the permanent sending off that would have happened before.

title: Aryna Sabalenka issues apology and denies Elina Svitolina abuse – will she be punished?
article_text:
Aryna Sabalenka has been forced to issue an apology after a major storm blew up around comments she appeared to make on court during her WTA Finals match against Ukrainian Elina Svitolina.

After crashing out of the tournament following a final set collapse against Svitolina, Sabalenka’s challenging 2026 season came to a shuddering halt.

Some commentators interpreted Belarusian Sabalenka’s comments as an insult towards Svitolina or Ukrainians in general, but she has insisted the comments were not directed at her opponent.

A little over 24 hours after those comments caused such a stir, Sabalenka issued a statement to try and downplay the comments.

“I want to clarify something from my recent match that has been circulating online,” she said.

“My comment was not directed at Elina. I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes, and I reacted emotionally in the moment.

“That said, I should have handled my frustration differently, and I apologise to anyone I offended.

“Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament.”

Sabalenka’s comments are likely to bring more eyes onto the story and prominent journalist Jon Wertheim was quick to give his pointed verdict on what needs to happen next.

“Lot of you writing about Sabalenka and the WTA,” said Wertheim.

A) The WTA *MUST* fine her. (The code even alludes to obscene/derogatory remarks made to fans, not just officials and opponents).

B) The $$ should be earmarked to a Ukrainian charity.

It remains to be seen whether Sabalenka’s public apology for her comments will end this story or add fuel to the controversy, with WTA chiefs now certain to be under pressure to respond to a story that is attracting huge interest.

This is also a story certain to be raised again when Sabalenka returns to action, with her apology unlikely to be enough for some of her critics.

title: Inside The Multimillion-Dollar Business Of Global Showjumping
article_text:
From multimillion-dollar horses and rising prize purses to team ownership and sponsorship deals, showjumping is attracting new investment. But turning sporting success into sustainable returns remains a challenge.

Elite showjumping is becoming an increasingly sophisticated business, with multimillion-dollar horses, international competitions, corporate sponsorships, and team-based leagues reshaping the sport's financial landscape. Yet the costs of competing at the highest level remain substantial, raising questions about whether growing commercial interest can translate into sustainable profits.

Jan Tops, founder and president of Longines Global Champions Tour and Global Champions League (GCL), told Forbes Middle East that staging a major international showjumping competition can cost $9 million (€8 million) or more.

His Longines Global Champions Tour, established in 2006, spans 17 events across four continents in 2026, offering more than $40.8 million (€36 million) in total prize money. This year's calendar includes stops in Doha, Miami Beach, Shanghai, Paris, and London, alongside a debut event in Cairo, held against the backdrop of the Pyramids of Giza in October.

Team-based competitions are reshaping showjumping's commercial model, allowing league operators to generate revenue from team participation while offering owners exposure to international championships.

The introduction of the GCL in 2016 added a team-based format, creating new commercial opportunities for organizers and investors. At Global Champions, team participation is a significant source of revenue.

Tops compared the model to Formula 1, where established teams compete within a global championship. "We sell teams like F1," Tops said, referring to teams such as Red Bull and Mercedes.

According to Tops, the GCL currently has 17 teams, each paying approximately $2.8 million (€2.5 million) annually to participate. In return, teams receive logistical support, including horse transportation and accommodation for riders and grooms, alongside VIP hospitality, international media exposure for sponsors, and opportunities for riders to compete for additional prize money.

The Middle East is also strengthening its presence in international showjumping, hosting major competitions that bring together leading riders, horse owners, and sponsors. Beyond Global Champions events, Qatar hosted the 2026 HH The Amir's Sword competition and CHI Al Shaqab, while the UAE staged a five-star FEI Jumping World Cup qualifier in Sharjah.

For team owners, however, participation fees are only one expense. Maintaining a competitive operation also requires access to elite horses, experienced riders, and the resources to compete throughout an international season.

Ludger Beerbaum, founder, owner, and manager of Riesenbeck International, told Forbes Middle East the financial viability of a team depends heavily on its competitive performance.

"If you can build a really strong team that’s always in the top three, four or five, there’s a good business case," Beerbaum said. “Performing on the GCL circuit significantly increases the profile of riders, hugely increasing the value of horses for team owners.”

Ludger’s team won the overall GCL Championship this season with total prize money of around $2.5 million (€2.3 million), in addition to the team’s other winnings.

The model is expanding beyond Europe. North America's Major League Show Jumping features eight teams competing in its 2026–27 season, reflecting the broader adoption of team-based formats.

Growing prize purses are creating additional earning opportunities for riders, teams, and horse owners, although returns remain closely tied to sporting performance.

Beerbaum said the GCL awards approximately $2.2 million (€2 million) to the overall championship winner, $1.6 million (€1.4 million) to the runner-up, and $1.1 million (€1 million) to the third-place team, in addition to prize money distributed at individual events.

"The prize money is, of course, the ongoing revenue," he said.

North America's Major League Show Jumping, meanwhile, allocates at least $100,000 to team competition at each event.

Individual competitions offer even larger prizes. Canada's 2026 Spruce Meadows Masters featured a $3.5 million (C$5 million) purse for its flagship CPKC International Grand Prix, while Germany's CHIO Aachen offered $1.7 million (€1.5 million) for its Rolex Grand Prix.

According to Beerbaum, an exceptional Grand Prix horse can earn $562,347 (€500,000) during a successful season, providing an incentive to retain a high-performing asset.

Horses are among the sport's most valuable assets, with prices driven by breeding, training, competitive performance, and future potential.

Tops said the value of elite showjumping horses has risen sharply over the past two decades, with comparable horses potentially commanding 10 times their previous prices.

"The challenges are getting access to these good horses. It's not easy. The really talented horses get more and more expensive," Beerbaum said.

Beerbaum regularly searches for promising young horses across major European equestrian markets, including Belgium, France, the Netherlands, and Germany.

At the 2026 Aloga Auction, which specializes in elite young showjumping horses, the average sale price reached $535,977 (€476,579), while the most expensive horse fetched $2.4 million (€2.1 million), according to the Irish Horse Board.

At Riesenbeck International, horse ownership is central to the business model. Owning some of its competing horses gives the organization greater control over sporting decisions while allowing it to retain a share of competition winnings.

Beerbaum said prize money is divided approximately equally between Riesenbeck International and external riders and horse owners.

"From all the prize money, around 50-50. Fifty percent is for external riders and owners, and the other 50% is for us," he explained.

Horse sales provide another revenue stream, although selling a successful horse can weaken a team's competitive position and reduce its future earning potential.

Beerbaum said Riesenbeck International typically sells one or two horses annually, weighing the financial benefits against the potential impact on sporting performance.

title: Bemidji State hops into NCAA's new advertising game, with more likely on the way
article_text:
BEMIDJI — On Jan. 23, the NCAA approved the use of sponsorship patches on uniforms in Division I sports for the first time.

Many universities took advantage early — Wisconsin reached a deal with Culver’s, Ohio State with JPMorgan Chase. Even the entire Big 12 conference reached a sponsorship/naming rights deal with Monster Energy.

But the new ruling applied to Division I sports only. That meant only the men's and women's hockey teams at Bemidji State had new real estate for sale.

As Bemidji State’s assistant director of athletics for development and sponsorship, Katz is in charge of recruiting companies for ads seen at places like the Sanford Center and Chet Anderson Stadium. After the ruling in January, he was tasked with finding a company to partner with that would benefit the hockey programs financially, but would also be a good fit.

It was also key for Katz and the school to avoid rushing into a partnership, a strategy that most D-I programs across the country have taken. Bigger schools like the University of Minnesota and North Dakota, for example, have yet to stitch ad patches.

“We had our mind set on it pretty early,” Katz said. “It was something that we wanted to advertise and get out there. And we still have opportunities available for a business to come in and put a logo on our jersey, and that’s something that we’re going to continue to explore, even as the season progresses.

“So I think we wanted to proceed quickly, but also with some caution.”

As soon as both hockey teams hit the ice in October, they donned their new jersey sponsor: Paul Bunyan Communications, featured on the left side of the chest on all jerseys.

Two more sponsorship opportunities are still available. Bemidji State can add one more patch on its jerseys and can have a helmet sponsor.

But finding new ad revenue hasn’t stopped at uniform sponsors. After the NCAA allowed ads on football fields in 2024, that paved the way for Bemidji State to partner with local companies to help fund the new turf at Chet Anderson Stadium.

Soon, Bemidji State expects the NCAA to allow jersey ads for D-II sports, opening the gates for more sponsorship deals for other sports on campus.

With changes come detractors. Traditionalists frown upon sponsorship patches, seeing their school's uniform as sacred. But even Notre Dame, perhaps the most traditional school in the country, now features a sponsor (Sofi Technologies) on its iconic football jerseys.

In a new era of college sports, schools are constantly seeking more revenue. That’s been taxing for some programs after the 2025 House settlement, which opened the doors for schools to pay their athletes money from Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) directly.

While BSU opted out of the House settlement, both its men’s and women’s hockey teams play against schools that have greater resources and more NIL opportunities for their players. Revenue from the jersey sponsorships goes directly to the programs.

“You find a sponsor patch for the women’s hockey program, and that funding is going towards the women’s hockey program," Katz said. "So it’s extremely important, whether that’s paying for pucks for the year, or tape, skates, helmets — whatever you need.”

Bemidji State has already seen how sponsors can help improve a particular aspect of a program. They’ve seen that happen just this year, when BSU replaced its aging turf at Chet Anderson Stadium with a new National Football League-approved turf, one of the first of its kind in D-II.

The funding for the field was achieved with the help of sponsors. Unlike on-ice advertisers at the Sanford Center, which can be easily replaced once their contracts are up, turf logos are permanent.

Helping BSU fund the project was appealing to many in the local businesses. First National Bank and Federated Insurance pitched in to help fund the new turf. Both companies now have their logos featured at every event at Chet Anderson Stadium, from BSU football, women's soccer and softball to Bemidji High School athletics.

“They were pretty quick turnarounds,” Katz said. “Utilizing corporate sponsors helped secure partial funding of the turf. We had some other donors that helped support it as well, but that’s ultimately where those sponsorship opportunities became a thing.”

The prospect of being featured on Bemidji State’s hockey jerseys also became appealing to Bemidji businesses. But finding a sponsor isn’t as simple as putting up a picture of a jersey on Facebook Marketplace saying “Place your ad here.”

Instead, it’s a combination of Katz reaching out to those in the Bemidji business community, and businesses reaching out to him.

“We are definitely aggressive when it comes to outreach,” he said. “There is a little bit of word of mouth, or wanting to reach out to us to learn a little bit more. I mean, I get emails and calls frequently from somebody who saw an advertisement at a hockey game or a football game and wanted to know how they could have an advertisement of their own.”

In the end, Paul Bunyan Communications, a longtime partner with Bemidji State hockey, became the first jersey sponsor in BSU history. Katz is still kicking tires on other deals as well, which could be added during the season.

title: Americas Complete Historic and Unprecedented Sweep in Europe
article_text:
On Saturday, November 14, 2026, rugby test teams from across the Americas secured a historic, unprecedented milestone. In matches played in five different European cities, all five of the senior men’s national teams from North and South America emerged victorious on the same day. Four of the matches were part of the World Rugby Nations Cup and one was part of the Nations Championship.

Starting in the north, Canada delivered a clinical second-half in Chambéry, France, beating Hong Kong 38–17. The second ranked North American team asserted its physicality and control against Asia 2 to secure a convincing 21-point victory. The result underscored Canada’s rebuilding trajectory and provided momentum as the program looks ahead to Australia 2027.

In Genoa, Argentina completed a 19–14 victory over Italy in the Nations Championship. Los Pumas looked visibly out of sorts for stretches, resembling a side that had only just come together, which was the reality of their preparation; yet, they still found a way to get the job done. Even when reduced to 13 players during a tense spell of yellow cards, Argentina’s defensive resilience held firm, conceding zero points while shorthanded to extend their unbeaten run against Italy to 19 years.

In Madrid, Chile claimed a landmark 25–20 triumph over Spain in the Nations Cup. The hard-fought victory marked Los Cóndores‘ first win over Spain since the 1990s, breaking a decades-long drought against their European rivals. By closing out a tight contest on Spanish soil, Chile demonstrated the composure and tactical maturity that has propelled Los Cóndores into a genuine emerging rugby nation.

In London, Uruguay maintained South America’s winning momentum by edging past Zimbabwe 20–15. Entering the World Rugby Nations Cup fixture as South America 2, Los Teros overcame a determined challenge from the Africa #2, relying on discipline and late-game execution to secure the five-point win on in neutral England.

Capping off the historic day in Bucharest, the USA Eagles delivered the most emphatic statement of all with a 53–24 rout of Romania. Running in seven tries, the Eagles retained the Pershing Cup and officially clinched their World Rugby Nations Cup pool title. The 29-point victory featured attacking play with the North Americans deservedly winning the contest by a big margin.

Saturday’s results are about more than a five-for-five sweep. Canada, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and the USA are confirmed competitors for Rugby World Cup 2027 in Australia, where they will look to carry their respective momentum onto rugby’s biggest stage.

Looking further ahead, the Americas will become the epicenter of world rugby: the USA, potentially including Vancouver, is set to host Rugby World Cup 2031, while Argentina is leading a joint South American bid with Chile, Uruguay, and Brazil to bring Rugby World Cup 2035 to the continent.

title: Sabalenka apologises for outrageous hot-mic moment
article_text:
Aryna Sabalenka has apologised on social media for her outburst on court that was caught on the cameras when she was defeated by Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells.

The footage that went viral showed the Belarusian tennis player swearing in Russian, that was interpreted as directly cursing Svitolina or Ukrainians in general.

However, the former world number one has now stated that she lost her cool due to the behaviour of spectators during Saturday’s 3-6, 6-3, 1-6 defeat and did not intend to directly call Svitolina a “Ukrainian bitch”.

“I want to clarify something from my recent match that has been circulating online,” Sabalenka wrote on her Instagram story.

“My comment was not directed at Elina. I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes, and I reacted emotionally in the moment. That said, I should have handled my frustration differently, and I apologise to anyone I offended.

“Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament.”

The four-time grand slam winner took her frustration out on her racquet and reacted to losing a point by crouching to the ground at the back of the court as a semi final place slipped away.

“It was an extremely tough match, especially mentally. I was just trying to play one point at a time,” Svitolina said.

"This is the tournament where you bring everything to the table and try to play every game as if it's the last."

Svitolina has refused to shake hands with tennis players from Russia and Belarus since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. She also stated the war was a reason her marriage with Gaël Monfils broke down last month.

French Open winner Mirra Andreeva also beat Jessica Pegula 6-3, 6-4 to book her WTA Finals title showdown with the former champion, Svitolina.

This hot-mic moment comes just a week after Pegula was caught on the practice stream at Indian Wells calling Andreeva a “diva”, causing the WTA to cease all streams and remove the footage from social media.

It has been reported the organisation only intended for the microphones to capture the sounds of rallies, not the conversations players had with coaches.

title: Alexander Zverev reacts after beating Rafael Jodar in his first match at the ATP Finals
article_text:
Alexander Zverev earned his first victory at the ATP Finals by defeating Rafael Jodar in straight sets in Turin.

Zverev served supremely as he beat the rising Spaniard 6-4, 6-4 to go top of the John McEnroe group and put himself in a good position to qualify for the knockout stages.

The German will now likely need one victory from his matches against Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils in order to reach the semifinals of the competition.

Zverev cut an upbeat figure on-court after the match in Turin, as he spoke about his feelings in getting his first victory of the 2026 ATP Finals campaign.

“Yeah very enjoyable. I’ve said it before, it’s been a very good year for me. A lot of things that I wanted to achieve that I’ve achieved this year,” said Zverev.

“Of course, by playing here, you never can take it for granted. There’s the best eight players in the world, of course excluding Jannik [Sinner], who is always right there.

“For me, yes it’s my ninth time playing the ATP Tour Finals, but it’s still always such a special tournament. I want to enjoy every single time I step on this court.

“I enjoyed today for sure. Winning always helps, but yeah it’s been a good match and hopefully I can continue doing that. To start the tournament with a 6-4, 6-4 win, it’s always very, very nice.

“I still think I have a lot of things to improve. It was not a perfect match, but to start the tournament I’m very happy. I’m looking forward to the next eight days to play good tennis on this court.”

Despite the straightforward nature of his victory against Jodar, Jamie Murray was not entirely convinced by Zverev’s performance in his first match.

“I think it was an impressive performance. I don’t think Sascha Zverev is walking off the court thinking: ‘I’ve played amazing there’,” said Murray on Sky Sports Tennis.

“I think he served god-like really. It was very impressive to sit courtside to see that up close and personal. I think he probably wasn’t feeling massively comfortable with his groundstrokes I think. But in the most important points he kind of stepped up.

“He was happy to take the ball on, play on his terms, and he got his rewards for that. I don’t think he was near his best from the baseline, that’s my feeling.”

Zverev and Jodar will next play on Tuesday, 17th November, against Fils and Shelton respectively. Jodar will likely have to win his next match in order to keep his tournament alive.

title: Unbeaten Errani, Paolini to battle Siniakova, Townsend for WTA Finals doubles crown
article_text:
Second seeds Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend will face No. 8 seeds Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini in the championship match at the FAGE WTA Finals in Indian Wells on Sunday after both teams advanced with straight-set victories in Saturday evening's semifinals.

In the first semifinal, Siniakova and Townsend edged top seeds Gabriela Dabrowski and Luisa Stefani in a closely contested opening set that featured no breaks of serve before completing a 7-6 (4), 6-3 victory in 1 hour, 40 minutes.

Siniakova and Townsend have now won all three meetings against Dabrowski and Stefani this season.

In the second semifinal, Errani and Paolini, the last team to qualify for the season-ending tournament, defeated No. 3 seeds Hanyu Guo and Kristina Mladenovic 6-3, 6-4 to advance to their first WTA Finals championship match.

The Italians, who won all three of their group-stage matches, remain unbeaten this week at Indian Wells. The victory also avenged a loss to Guo and Mladenovic in the quarterfinals of the Indian Wells WTA 1000 event earlier this season, when Guo and Mladenovic prevailed in a match tiebreak.

Final showdown: Siniakova, Townsend vs. Errani, Paolini

Siniakova and Townsend are competing at the WTA Finals for the third consecutive year and have advanced beyond the group stage on all three occasions. Sunday's championship match will be their second as a team, having finished runners-up in 2024.

The Czech-American duo have won five titles this season, including Roland Garros, the US Open, Madrid, Miami and Indian Wells.

Townsend is seeking her first WTA Finals title in her third appearance, while Siniakova is competing at the season-ending tournament for the eighth time. The Czech previously won the doubles title in 2021 with countrywoman Barbora Krejcikova.

Errani and Paolini, meanwhile, are competing at the WTA Finals for the third consecutive year and have advanced beyond the group stage for the first time as a team.

Paolini is making her third consecutive appearance, all alongside Errani, while Errani had previously qualified for the tournament three times with compatriot Roberta Vinci. Both Italians have reached the championship match for the first time.

This season, Errani and Paolini won the title in Tokyo and finished runners-up in Miami.

Siniakova and Townsend defeated the Italians in the finals of the Indian Wells and Miami WTA 1000 events earlier in the season. However, Errani and Paolini turned the tables in their group-stage encounter this week, prevailing in a match tiebreak.

Sunday's final will be their fourth meeting of the season, with Siniakova and Townsend holding a 2-1 advantage.

title: Lakshya Sen overcomes Farhan to storm into Kumamoto Masters Japan final
article_text:
moved into the final of the Kumamoto Masters, overcoming sixth seed and world No. 10 Alwi Farhan of Indonesia on Saturday. The world No. 13 Indian prevailed 21-12, 15-21, 21-11 in a 70-minute encounter, recovering from a second-game setback and dominating the decider.

Fresh from his triumph at the Hylo Open, it's Lakshya's second consecutive final and third of the season on the BWF World Tour. The victory also marked a personal breakthrough, as he registered his maiden international win over Farhan. The Indian had lost both their previous encounters without managing to take a single game.

"I was looking to better the result from last time and am happy with the way I played today. Now it's time to recover and get ready for a tough match tomorrow," Lakshya said. He will face Japan's Koki Watanabe, who registered a 14-21, 21-11, 23-21 victory against second seed Kunlavut Vitidsarn of Thailand.

Lakshya also boosted his prospects of qualifying for the season-ending BWF World Tour Finals in Hangzhou. Currently 12th in the World Tour standings with 64,980 points, the Indian needs to break into the top eight to secure his place in the tournament. A title triumph in Kumamoto would fetch him 9,200 points, while a runner-up finish would earn him 7,800, either of which is expected to significantly strengthen his qualification prospects.

However, the final standings could still be influenced by the Hong Kong Open Super 500 and Syed Modi International Super 300, the remaining tournaments on the calendar.

Against an opponent renowned for his attacking game, Lakshya displayed tactical awareness in the opening game. He patiently controlled the rallies, varied his strokes and waited for opportunities to attack. He made an immediate impression with a 3-0 lead, using precise returns and repeatedly targeting the Indonesian's forehand.

Lakshya established control, and he carried an 11-7 advantage into the mid-game interval. On resumption, the Indian tightened his grip with sharp net interceptions and winners in flat exchanges. Moving ahead to 17-9, he capitalised on a succession of unforced errors from Farhan to close out the opening game.

Who do you think will win the final match between Lakshya Sen and Koki Watanabe?

Farhan, however, responded strongly in the second game. Lakshya initially produced one of the rallies of the match, retrieving everything during an extraordinary 57-shot exchange at 1-2 before Farhan eventually found the net. But the Indonesian gradually found his rhythm.

The third game, however, belonged to Lakshya. He built an early 5-2 lead and maintained his advantage at 8-5 with a thunderous smash. Farhan subsequently required a medical timeout to attend to a bleeding finger, but the interruption did little to disturb the Indian's concentration.

Lakshya unleashed his trademark jump smashes and capitalised on a close line call to take an authoritative 11-6 lead at the change of ends. He then produced a series of lethal down-the-line smashes to stretch his advantage to 15-7. A net error from the Indonesian handed the Indian 10 match points, and he sealed the contest with an emphatic smash.

title: The Annika: Lottie Woad in the mix as Lindy Duncan edges closer to first-ever LPGA Tour victory
article_text:
Lindy Duncan edged closer towards her first LPGA Tour victory on Saturday as the American made 17 pars in a flawless bogey-free round to take a one-shot lead at The Annika.

On a cold and blustery day at Pelican Golf Club, the 35-year-old, who joined the tour in 2014, took the 54-hole lead by shooting a four-under 69.

Overnight co-leader Hye-Jin Choi was tied at the top until she missed the 18th green to the left but did well to get down in three for a bogey and a 70, and finished one stroke back from Duncan.

England's Lottie Woad tied a group of six players - including world No 1 Nelly Korda - at seven under par, with the European Solheim Cup player twinning two birdies and two bogeys to wrap up her day at level par.

Charley Hull endured a difficult day, with the 30-year-old posting six bogeys to finish with a 76 and fall down to tied-43rd on the leaderboard at one under par.

Yuri Yoshida, who won her first LPGA title during the recent Asia swing, played alongside Korda and had a 67, leaving her two shots off the lead.

Ina Yoon of South Korea (69) was three behind and double major winner Haeran Ryo went from eight shots behind to four back with a Saturday-low 65.

Duncan, who made her debut at the Solheim Cup at age 35 and is making her 222nd career start on the LPGA Tour without winning, was at 13-under 197. The American's lone birdie came at the par-four 11th hole, after striking a seven-iron to 18 feet.

Her final act was 50ft putt over a green that looked more like bunny slopes, three ridges to cover. Duncan nearly holed it and then rapped in a 3-footer for a par to polish off a clean card.

"Today was a really tough day with the wind," Duncan said.

"The greens firm up, so I was really just trying to hit the ball in spots where you could at least hit the green or have a reasonable chip."

Greens are the defence at Pelican Golf Club, and some of the pins were in their toughest positions. Carlota Ciganda, who shared the 54-hole lead with Choi and Duncan, three-putted five times, including the 18th.

That was a big help to Duncan, who was roughly on the same line as Ciganda.

"I also thought she hit it a lot harder and it didn't go that far past, so I definitely think seeing her putt helped make mine a little easier," Duncan said.

"For that one to kind of skim the edge was pretty cool."

The 18th took a toll on just about everyone, playing all the way back into the wind.

World No 1 Nelly Korda also struggled in the trying conditions.

Korda three-putted down the ridge on the 18th for a bogey that gave her a 71 and left her six shots behind. A win can see the world No 1 qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame.

She wasn't at her best on Saturday. The 28-year-old took a double bogey on the sixth hole by going over the green into the pine straw, chipping down a ridge and off the green, taking three to get down from there.

On her back nine, Korda carded two birdies and two bogeys, also coming unstuck on the par-four 18th.

Along with trying to win, Duncan still is not eligible for the season-ending CME Group Tour Championship next week, where the winner of the top 60 players who qualify gets £1.5m ($2m). A strong finish, even without winning, gets her there.

Choi has no such concerns about the season finale. She just wants to win, and two runner-up finishes during the Asia swing have helped her confidence.

"I'm just going to try to concentrate to the end," Choi said.

title: DP World Tour Championship: Which players secured PGA Tour cards via the Race to Dubai and have dual membership in 2027?
article_text:
"What we saw more of is McIlroy resilience. He does this often, in his whole career he resets. He always bounces back from disappointments.

"In the big context of his career, some of his biggest disappointments in the game have been followed by great surges by form and wins shortly afterwards.

"We saw him at The Masters, we talk about when he completed the Grand Slam [in 2025], he lost it three times, but fortunately won it four times.

"Every time he made a mistake he was able to bounce back. Again, he's done it today, he's done it so often in his career.

"It's almost like, I described it as 'catching the mouse'. He catches it and plays with it and rather than kill it and move forward and move like Tyrrell [Hatton] did into the distance, he seems to regress.

"And then he says: 'Now I want to go again'. And he goes again!

"That seems to be something that is very repeatable for him. He's able to play around and then get extra motivation to get back and go again.

"That's what he did today. He lost the initiative yesterday. With a two-point lead, he had this tournament in the grasp of his hand and we thought he was going to do what Tyrrell was going to do, which is move off into the distance.

"He didn't, he regressed, and then when you regress far enough, rather than keep going, he bounced back again.

"That's much to be admired, it's a very difficult thing to do as a professional golfer."

title: Sponsor Invite Disqualified For Using Illegal Green-Reading Book On Tour Debut
article_text:
University of Miami golfer Scarlett Schremmer has been disqualified from The Annika due to using an illegal green-reading book during competition.

Making her LPGA Tour debut after Kai Trump was forced to withdraw due to injury, Schremmer shot 69 and 74 to miss the cut anyway at Pelican Golf Club before the transgression was confirmed.

According to Golfweek's Beth Ann Nichols, who broke the story, the LPGA Tour initially learned of Schremmer's potential violation after her playing partners reported the issue following round one, but officials failed to take action until the weekend.

In a statement confirming the young talent's disqualification, the LPGA Tour said: "Schremmer violated Model Local Rule G-11, which, per the LPGA Rules of Play Card, is in effect during all LPGA Tour competitions, except at off-site local qualifying events.

"This Model Local Rule requires that players are limited throughout their round to using only the yardage book that has been approved for use in the competition."

The 20-year-old was paired with France's Perrine Delacour and South Korea's Dongeun Lee on Thursday and Friday while she also had her mother - former LPGA player Patricia Ehrhart - as her caddie.

Per Golfweek, Schremmer initially denied using an illegal green-reading book but later changed her stance once photo evidence was submitted to the LPGA Tour.

Schremmer provided a statement to Golfweek which read: "I had a green reading yardage book in my bag this week that’s allowed in college golf but isn’t permitted on the LPGA Tour.

"That’s on me. I should have checked, and it’s a lesson learned.

"I had a great week competing out here and I’m grateful to the Doyle family, Pelican and the LPGA for the opportunity.

"I am excited to continue to work with the goal of playing out here again. Thank you to everyone who came out and supported me this week."

The Miami sophomore has won twice this fall and is also a member of the USGA’s 2026 Elite Amateur Program. She has also twice competed in the Augusta National Women's Amateur.

Jonny Leighfield is our Staff News Writer who joined Golf Monthly just in time for the 2023 Solheim Cup and Ryder Cup. He graduated from the University of Brighton with a degree in Sport Journalism in 2017 and spent almost five years as the sole sports reporter at his local newspaper. During his time with Golf Monthly, Jonny has interviewed several stars of the game, including Robert MacIntyre, Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood, and Joaquin Niemann. An improving golfer himself, Jonny enjoys learning as much about the game as he can and recently reached his Handicap goal of 18 for the first time.

title: Brilliant USA Eagles Dominate Romania in Bucharest
article_text:
The USA Men’s Eagles were big winners in Bucharest on Saturday. A brilliant performance from the North Americans resulted in a 53-24 victory that included six Eagles tries and saw them completing a fifth victory in the 2026 World Rugby Nations Cup tournament.

The Eagles started well. Just three minutes into the match, Chris Hilsenbeck slotted a penalty goal. Romania went close to scoring the opening try in response but were held-up. Having come away without conceding points, the USA then made Romania pay with Hilsenbeck kicking long for winger Noah Brown to score.

Further points followed with the Eagles going 15-0 ahead. This time Oscar Lennon combined with Rufus McLean as the former Scotland international crossed.

The remainder of the first-half was more competitive. The Stejarii fought back to convert possession into points in the 26th minute. Iliesa Tiqe scored to make it a 10 point deficit. The USA then made the shots pay for a mistake with Perry Mayo scoring and Hilsenbeck converting for a 22-15 lead.

The Eastern Europeans regathered to end the first-half on a high. Following good work from Nicolas Onuțu, the Stejarii were on the attack from a lineout. They set up a lineout to maul from which captain Cristi Boboc scored.

The USA were 22–10 up as the second-half got underway. They took little time to add to this as Jason Damm scored from a pick-and-go. Hilsenbeck converted for 29–10.

The Stejarii were unable to fight-back as the Eagles’ defense proved to be too strong. Then second-rower Nathan Den Hoedt followed his captain’s example to power over. Hilsenbeck again converted and the North Americans were in control, leading 36–10.

When center Tavite Lopeti scored the result was beyond doubt at 43–10. The well-taken try featured an up-and-under and a good break down the left from Lopeti’s fellow center, Dom Besag.

The hosts did manage to run in late tries but it was too late. Rufus McLean added a second before the final score went the way of Romania with Adrian Mitu crossing and replacement Alin Conache converting.

The victory sees the USA Eagles securing the Pershing Cup and also the World Rugby Nations Cup Pool B trophy.

title: Uruguay See Off Zimbabwe in World Rugby Nations Cup
article_text:
Uruguay were 20-15 winners over Zimbabwe on Saturday in what was the first-ever rugby test match between the two countries. The hard-fought win saw energetic play from both teams and four first-half tries but none in the second-half.

Los Teros started the contest strongly. Center Juan Manuel Alonso scored in the 7th minute. The try had a centennial connection as Mateo Sanguinetti put in the assist pass in what was his 100th test match for Uruguay. His over the shoulder flick pass came after an excellent carry from Felipe Aliaga. Ícaro Amarillo added the conversion and Uruguay’s players had their heads up.

Zimbabwe responded to open their account on 13 minutes. Jason Robertson landed a penalty for a 7-3 deficit. The Sables then went ahead after a pair of rapid-fire tries from Tino Mavesere and Godfrey Muzanargwo. Suddenly, the Africans were 15-7 up after 25 minutes.

Uruguay successfully held their lines for the remainder of the match. Los Teros also scored thirteen points of their own. The next score was a well-taken opportunity in the right corner. With a man over, Juan Manuel Alonso passed to his right and the ball bounced well for Juan González. The Worcester Warriors winger just managed to get the ball down.

Zimbabwe held a 15-14 lead at half-time. Uruguay’s fight back started early with Ícaro Amarillo putting the South Americans back in the lead in the 43rd minute. It was one of just two point-scoring moments of the half. The other was another Amarillo penalty two minutes before the close of the third quarter.

Uruguayan captain Manuel Leindekar was happy to play out the remainder of the match. Rather than kick for the corner, he twice had Amarillo attempt penalties from inside his own half. Amarillo missed two which meant the contest concluded with five points separating the teams.

Zimbabwe will play another South American team next weekend when they take on the in-form Chile. That match will be played at Stade Chanzy in Angoulême, France. Meanwhile, Los Teros travel to Lisbon to face Portugal. Both matches will be played next Saturday.

- The match opened international competition between Zimbabwe and Uruguay.

- Mateo Sanguinetti earned his 100th test cap, becoming the 2nd Uruguayan centurion after Diego Magno.

- Faustino Etchegorry and Manuel Parodi debuted for Uruguay.
